analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and nursing homes to use mechanical lifts instead of manually lifting patients.
analysis.headline: The bill to protect nurses from back injuries was introduced in October 2009, received one subcommittee hearing, and died in committee without ever getting a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Labor Department to write a safety rule requiring health care employers to use mechanical lifting devices instead of manually lifting patients, except when that would compromise patient care. Employers would have to write safe-patient-handling plans, train staff annually, keep injury records, and post notices explaining workers' rights. Workers could refuse unsafe lifting assignments, report violations, and sue if fired for doing so. A $200 million grant program would help financially strapped facilities buy the equipment [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Direct-care nurses and other health care workers who lift and move patients all day. The bill's findings cite 2007 data showing registered nurses filed 8,580 back and muscle injury cases that caused missed work and nursing aides 24,340, the second-highest of any occupation. Patients also benefit, because the findings state mechanical lift programs reduce skin tears and the frequency of patients being dropped [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to buy and maintain an adequate number of safe-lift mechanical devices within two years of a final rule, and to eliminate manual lifting except where patient care would be compromised [S3].

Gives workers the right to refuse a lifting assignment that violates the safety standard or for which they were not trained, and bars employers from firing, disciplining, or reporting them to state licensing boards for refusing [S3].
Creates whistleblower protections and a court cause of action with reinstatement, back pay, and attorneys' fees for workers retaliated against for reporting violations [S3].
Authorizes $200 million in grants, including $50 million set aside for home health agencies, to help facilities that demonstrate financial need buy the required equipment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies, and other health care employers, who would bear the cost of buying lift equipment, writing plans, and training staff, offset in part by federal grants for facilities showing financial need [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, home health agencies

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on health care employers, including financially strained nursing homes and rural clinics; the grant program only covers facilities that demonstrate financial need, and its $200 million authorization would still require Congress to actually appropriate the money [S3].

The manual-lifting exception is judgment-based: the standard applies only where using mechanical devices is feasible and 'where the use of safe patient handling practices can be demonstrated to compromise patient care' it is excepted, which employers could use to argue out of compliance in difficult cases [S3].
Facilities not covered by OSHA would be brought in through Medicare participation conditions under the Social Security Act, adding a new compliance obligation tied to their federal funding [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The injury numbers in the bill's own findings are large, and the bill notes that facilities that adopted lift equipment saw injuries, lost workdays, turnover, and workers' compensation costs decline, meaning much of the equipment cost can be recovered. The real costs are upfront equipment purchases and paperwork, softened by grants for needy facilities. The main honest objection is that a one-size federal standard may be hard for small or financially strapped facilities and that the exception for patient care leaves room for employer discretion.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent the bill to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which held one subcommittee hearing in May 2010, and the bill never advanced to a committee vote or the Senate floor before the Congress ended in January 2011 [S5] [S1].

narrative.text: Senator Al Franken introduced the bill on October 15, 2009, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
Three Senate Democrats cosponsored the bill [S4].
On May 11, 2010, the HELP Committee's Subcommittee on Employment and Workplace Safety held a hearing on the bill, with a printed hearing record [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup or a vote in either chamber, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health care employers, chiefly hospitals, nursing homes, and home health agencies, avoided the equipment purchase, training, and reporting requirements, and the lift-equipment makers lost the customer base the mandate would have created. Nurses and aides kept facing the manual lifting that produces tens of thousands of back injuries a year.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care employers who avoided compliance costs

industries.industry: Hospitals, nursing homes, and home health agencies
industries.note: They would have had to buy mechanical lift equipment, write safety plans, train staff annually, and keep injury records, with grants only for facilities showing financial need. Their resistance interest runs against the nurses and aides whose manual lifting causes tens of thousands of injuries a year.

industries.industry: Patient lift and handling equipment manufacturers
industries.note: The mandate would have required every covered employer to purchase and maintain safe-lift devices, creating a large guaranteed market. Because the bill died, that demand never materialized.

The bill's findings note that assistive lifting technology reduces workers' compensation costs for musculoskeletal disorders, so claims and premiums would likely fall, though any short-term compliance costs could raise facility expenses.
